name: Melidoni Cave
seoTitle: Melidoni Cave, Crete: Stalactites, the 1824 Massacre and Visiting
seoDescription: Melidoni Cave lies 30 minutes east of Rethymno: a large stalactite chamber that was a Minoan cult site and, in 1824, the scene of a massacre of sheltering villagers.
summary: Melidoni Cave sits above the village of Melidoni in the Mylopotamos hills, about 30 minutes east of Rethymno. It is a single large stalactite chamber rather than a network of passages, reached down a stepped path, and it has been in use since the Neolithic period: a Minoan and later Greek cult site associated with the bronze giant Talos, and a place of refuge for the surrounding villages. In 1824 several hundred villagers, mostly women and children, sheltered here from Ottoman forces and died when fires were lit at the entrance. An ossuary and an altar inside the main chamber commemorate them, and the cave is a place of pilgrimage as much as a tourist site.
body:
## The cave

The visit is short and vertical rather than long and horizontal. Steps descend from the entrance into the Hall of Heroes, a chamber tens of metres across with a high roof, hung with stalactites and columns built up over many thousands of years. It is lit, the air is cool and damp all year, and the floor is uneven in places. There is no crawling and no caving equipment involved.

## History

Excavation has produced material from the Neolithic period onwards. In antiquity the cave was a place of worship, connected in local tradition with Talos, the bronze guardian of Crete, and inscriptions to Hermes Tallaios have been found here.

The modern history is the reason most visitors come. In 1824, during the Greek War of Independence, around 370 villagers took refuge in the cave. Ottoman troops sealed and lit fires at the mouth, and everyone inside suffocated. Their remains are kept in an ossuary in the main chamber, beneath a marble monument and beside an altar where services are held.

## Where it fits

Melidoni is in the Mylopotamos foothills between Rethymno and Heraklion, half an hour from Rethymno. It pairs naturally with Arkadi Monastery, ancient Eleftherna and the pottery village of Margarites, all within the same short circuit of hill country and all telling versions of the same story about resistance and continuity.

## Practicalities

An entrance fee is charged and paid on site; the operator does not publish the amount. The path down and back is stepped and can be slippery, so wear shoes with grip. The chamber is cool even in August, which makes it a good stop in high summer. Half an hour inside is enough.

faqs.a: In 1824, during the Greek War of Independence, around 370 villagers from the surrounding area took refuge in the cave. Ottoman troops lit fires at the entrance and all of them suffocated. Their remains are kept in an ossuary in the main chamber.

faqs.q: How far is Melidoni Cave from Rethymno?
faqs.a: About 30 km east, roughly 30 minutes by car, in the Mylopotamos hills.

faqs.q: Is Melidoni Cave hard to get into?
faqs.a: No. It is a lit, developed cave entered by a stepped path, with no crawling and no equipment needed. The steps are uneven and can be slippery, so shoes with grip help.
There is an admission charge collected at the site and paid on the day. It is not included in tour prices, and the amount is not published on the tour pages.

faqs.q: Is it worth visiting with children?
faqs.a: Yes, if they are steady on steps. The chamber is large, cool and impressive, and the visit is short. The history is grim and worth deciding in advance how much of it to tell.
